title: Lifting The Maximally-entangledness Assumption In Robust Self-testing For Synchronous Games
authors: Matthijs Vernooij And Yuming Zhao
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2222 (2026).

Robust self-testing in non-local games allows a classical referee to certify that two untrustworthy players are able to perform a specific quantum strategy up to high precision. Proving robust self-testing results becomes significantly easier when one restricts the allowed strategies to symmetric projective maximally entangled (PME) strategies, which allow natural descriptions in terms of tracial von Neumann algebras. This has been exploited in the celebrated [MATH] paper and related articles to prove robust self-testing results for synchronous games when restricting to PME strategies. However, the PME assumptions are not physical, so these results need to be upgraded to make them physically relevant. In this work, we do just that: we prove that any perfect synchronous game which is a robust self-test when restricted to PME strategies, is in fact a robust self-test for all strategies. We then apply our result to the Quantum Low Degree Test to find an efficient [MATH]-qubit test.

.
tldr: The paper proves that robust self-testing for synchronous non-local games under symmetric projective maximally entangled strategies can be lifted to all strategies, and applies this to the Quantum Low Degree Test.
motivation: Robust self-testing is a key primitive for device-independent certification, but existing proofs often rely on the unphysical assumption of maximally entangled symmetric strategies, limiting their physical relevance.
method: The authors develop a general lifting argument that removes the PME assumption for perfect synchronous games, then instantiate it in the Quantum Low Degree Test to obtain an efficient qubit test.
result: Any perfect synchronous game that is a robust self-test restricted to PME strategies is shown to be a robust self-test for all strategies, yielding an efficient qubit test via the Quantum Low Degree Test.
conclusion: This work substantially broadens the applicability of robust self-testing results for synchronous games, making them physically meaningful and enabling new efficient certification protocols.

title: Escaping The Shadow Of Bell’s Theorem In Network Nonlocality
authors: Maria Ciudad Alañón, Emanuel-Cristian Boghiu, Paolo Abiuso, And Elie Wolfe
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2213 (2026).

The possibility of nonclassicality in networks unrelated to Bell’s original eponymous theorem has recently attracted significant interest. Here, we identify a sufficient condition for being “outside the shadow of Bell’s theorem” and introduce a testable criterion capable of certifying the novelty of instances of network-nonclassicality which we call minimal network nonclassicality. We provide examples of minimally network nonclassical correlations realizable in quantum theory as well as examples coming from more exotic operational probabilistic theories. In particular, we apply these concepts to the simplest configuration of the 3-chain scenario (a.k.a. the bilocality scenario) to prove that certain correlations have escaped the shadow of Bell's theorem. While some of the examples herein are unprecedented, we also revisit more familiar examples of network nonclassicality in order to highlight the contrast between our approach versus prior approaches with respect to assessing novelty.

.
tldr: Introduces a sufficient condition and testable criterion called minimal network nonclassicality to certify when network nonlocality cannot be explained by Bell's theorem, with applications to the bilocality scenario.
motivation: Network nonclassicality has attracted interest, but there is a need to distinguish genuinely novel network effects from those that are merely Bell-type nonlocality in disguise.
method: The authors define minimal network nonclassicality, derive a sufficient condition for being outside the shadow of Bell's theorem, and apply it to the 3-chain (bilocality) scenario, including examples from quantum theory and exotic operational probabilistic theories.
result: They show specific correlations in the bilocality scenario are minimally network nonclassical and hence escape Bell's theorem, and they contrast this approach with prior novelty assessments.
conclusion: This framework provides a rigorous way to certify the novelty of network-nonclassical correlations and clarifies their relationship to Bell nonlocality.

title: Fast Bosonic Control Via Multiphoton Qubit-Oscillator Interactions
authors: Noah Gorgichuk, Mohammad Ayyash, Matteo Mariantoni, And Sahel Ashhab
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2224 (2026).

We study the problem of [MATH]-fold rotationally symmetric bosonic state preparation, which is of great importance to bosonic quantum error correction, using a multiphoton interaction between an oscillator and an auxiliary qubit. We present an [MATH]-photon Law-Eberly ([MATH]LE) protocol that serves as an analytic baseline, alongside numerical optimal control calculations that further reduce state preparation time. We find that multiphoton control protocols substantially reduce preparation times for binomial, cat, and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill codewords compared to schemes relying on standard linear interactions. Further, we achieve arbitrary control over the oscillator's Hilbert space by combining different multiphoton interaction orders. We also extend these control improvements to the preparation of rotationally symmetric multi-oscillator states. Lastly, numerical simulations using realistic planar superconducting circuit parameters validate the robustness of our scheme against qubit and oscillator decoherence. Our findings can significantly enhance the performance of bosonic codes on planar superconducting hardware, an important ingredient for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computers.

.
tldr: The paper develops fast bosonic state preparation protocols using multiphoton qubit-oscillator interactions, achieving reduced preparation times for bosonic codewords and robustness in superconducting circuits.
motivation: Bosonic quantum error correction requires efficient preparation of rotationally symmetric states, but standard linear interactions are often too slow.
method: They introduce an N-photon Law-Eberly protocol as an analytic baseline and numerical optimal control to design faster multiphoton control sequences; they combine different multiphoton orders for arbitrary oscillator control and extend the approach to multi-oscillator states, validating with realistic superconducting circuit parameters.
result: Multiphoton protocols substantially reduce preparation times for binomial, cat, and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill codewords, enable arbitrary control over the oscillator Hilbert space, and remain robust against qubit and oscillator decoherence.
conclusion: These findings can significantly enhance bosonic code performance on planar superconducting hardware, an important ingredient for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computers.

Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 40, October 2026.

tldr: The paper introduces twisted Rényi negativity as a reliable proxy for quantifying mixed-state entanglement in fermionic systems.
motivation: Quantifying entanglement in realistic finite-temperature mixed states, especially for fermionic systems, remains a significant challenge.
method: The authors propose a twisted Rényi negativity measure and analyze its properties and reliability as an entanglement proxy for fermionic mixed states.
result: Twisted Rényi negativity is shown to serve as a reliable and computable proxy for mixed-state entanglement in fermionic systems.
conclusion: This work provides a practical tool for detecting and quantifying entanglement in finite-temperature fermionic environments, advancing entanglement theory.

title: Non-stabilizerness And Violations Of Chsh Inequalities
authors: Stefano Cusumano, Lorenzo Campos Venuti, Simone Cepollaro, Immacolata de Simone, Gianluca Esposito, Daniele Iannotti, Barbara Jasser, Jovan Odavić, Michele Viscardi, And Alioscia Hamma
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2214 (2026).

We study quantitatively the interplay between entanglement and non-stabilizer resources in violating the CHSH inequalities. We show that, while non-stabilizer resources are necessary, they must have a specific structure, namely they need to be both asymmetric and (surprisingly) [MATH]. We employ stabilizer entropy (SE) to quantify the non-stabilizer resources involved and the probability of violation given the resources. We show how spectral quantities related to the flatness of entanglement spectrum and its relationship with non-local SE affect the CHSH inequality. Finally, we utilize these results – together with tools from representation theory – to construct a systematic way of building ensembles of states with higher probability of violation.

.
tldr: This paper quantitatively links non-stabilizer resources, entanglement, and CHSH inequality violations, showing that non-stabilizerness must be asymmetric and non-local and providing a representation-theoretic way to build state ensembles with higher violation probability.
motivation: Bell nonlocality and quantum resource theories are central to quantum information, but the precise role of non-stabilizer resources beyond entanglement in CHSH violations is not fully understood.
method: The authors use stabilizer entropy to quantify non-stabilizer resources, analyze spectral properties of the entanglement spectrum, and employ representation theory to construct ensembles of states.
result: They find that non-stabilizer resources necessary for CHSH violation must have a specific asymmetric and non-local structure, and that flatness of the entanglement spectrum affects violation probability.
conclusion: The work clarifies the interplay between entanglement, magic, and nonlocality and offers tools for engineering state ensembles with higher CHSH violation probability.

title: Spatial Structure Of Multipartite Entanglement At Measurement Induced Phase Transitions
authors: James Allen And William Witczak-Krempa
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2211 (2026).

We study multiparty entanglement near measurement induced phase transitions (MIPTs), which arise in ensembles of local quantum circuits built with unitaries and measurements. In contrast to equilibrium quantum critical transitions, where entanglement is short-ranged, MIPTs possess long-range k-party genuine multiparty entanglement (GME) characterized by an infinite hierarchy of entanglement exponents for k[MATH]2. First, we represent the average spread of entanglement with "entanglement clusters", and use them to conjecture general exponent relations: 1) classical dominance, 2) monotonicity, 3) subadditivity. We then introduce measure-weighted graphs to construct such clusters in general circuits. Second, we obtain the exact entanglement exponents for a 1d MIPT in a measurement-only circuit that maps to percolation by exploiting non-unitary conformal field theory. The exponents, which we numerically verify, obey the inequalities. We also extend the construction to a 2d MIPT that maps to classical 3d percolation, and numerically find the first entanglement exponents. Our results provide a firm ground to understand the multiparty entanglement of MIPTs, and more general ensembles of quantum circuits.

.
tldr: The paper characterizes the spatial structure of multipartite entanglement near measurement-induced phase transitions, deriving exact entanglement exponents via non-unitary conformal field theory and percolation mappings.
motivation: Measurement-induced phase transitions exhibit long-range genuine multiparty entanglement with an infinite hierarchy of exponents, unlike equilibrium critical points, but the general structure and relations among these exponents remain poorly understood.
method: The authors introduce entanglement clusters and measure-weighted graphs to represent the average spread of entanglement in local quantum circuits, conjecture exponent relations, and compute exact exponents for a 1D measurement-only circuit mapped to percolation via non-unitary CFT, with numerical extension to a 2D circuit mapping to 3D percolation.
result: They obtain exact entanglement exponents for the 1D case, numerically verify them, and find the first exponents for the 2D case; the exponents obey conjectured relations of classical dominance, monotonicity, and subadditivity.
conclusion: The work provides a firm foundation for understanding multiparty entanglement structure in MIPTs and more general ensembles of quantum circuits, linking entanglement theory to percolation and non-unitary CFT.

title: Certified Quantum Advantage In Entanglement-assisted Prepare-measure Random-access-code
authors: Prabuddha Roy And A K Pan Rajdeep Paul
abstract: We develop a family of semi-device-independent (SDI) entanglement-assisted prepare-measure (PM) communication games involving two parties, within the random-access code (RAC) framework where the sender Alice holds a -bit string and communicates bits or qubits to the receiver Bob. In contrast to the standard quantum PMRAC, here the parties share a prior entanglement, and Alice applies quantum operations on her sub-system to encode her inputs and sends to Bob. We first consider the entanglement-assisted PMRAC with and and derive the optimal quantum success probabilities using an elegant analytical technique. We demonstrate quantum supremacy over both classical RACs and conventional quantum PMRACs. Moreover, we exhibit that the optimal quantum advantage allows one to certify Alice’s unitary operations. We then derive an upper bound on the quantum success probabilities for entanglement-assisted PMRAC with and . Further, we extend the demonstration of quantum advantage for case where is arbitrary.
tldr: The paper develops semi-device-independent entanglement-assisted prepare-measure random-access codes and derives optimal quantum success probabilities that certify quantum advantage and Alice's unitary operations.
motivation: Random-access codes are fundamental communication tasks, and entanglement assistance plus semi-device-independent certification can enable stronger quantum advantages than classical or conventional quantum prepare-measure RACs.
method: The authors analytically derive optimal quantum success probabilities for entanglement-assisted PMRACs with small parameters, obtain upper bounds for larger cases, and extend the demonstration to arbitrary parameter regimes.
result: They show quantum supremacy over both classical RACs and standard quantum PMRACs, and demonstrate that the optimal quantum advantage can be used to certify Alice's unitary operations.
conclusion: Entanglement-assisted prepare-measure RACs provide certified quantum advantages and a route to semi-device-independent certification of quantum operations.

title: Strict Hierarchy Between $n$-wise Measurement Simulability, Compatibility Structures, And Multi-copy Compatibility
authors: Lucas Tendick, Costantino Budroni, And Marco Túlio Quintino
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2231 (2026).

The incompatibility of quantum measurements, i.e. the fact that certain observable quantities cannot be measured jointly is widely regarded as a distinctive quantum feature with important implications for the foundations and the applications of quantum information theory. While the standard incompatibility of multiple measurements has been the focus of attention since the inception of quantum theory, its generalizations, such as measurement simulability, [MATH]-wise incompatibility, and mulit-copy incompatibility have only been proposed recently. Here, we point out that all these generalizations are differing notions of the question of how many measurements are genuinely contained in a measurement device. We then show, that all notions do differ not only in their operational meaning but also mathematically in the set of measurement assemblages they describe. We then fully resolve the relations between these different generalizations, by showing a strict hierarchy between these notions. Hence, we provide a general framework for generalized measurement incompatibility. Finally, we consider the implications our results have for recent works using these different notions.

.
tldr: The paper establishes a strict hierarchy between measurement simulability, n-wise incompatibility, and multi-copy incompatibility, showing these generalized notions of quantum measurement incompatibility are mathematically and operationally distinct.
motivation: Generalizations of measurement incompatibility have been proposed recently, but their mutual relations and precise operational meanings remained unclear; this work aims to clarify how many measurements are genuinely contained in a measurement device.
method: The authors analyze the sets of measurement assemblages described by each generalized notion and derive strict inclusions among them, providing a unified framework for generalized measurement incompatibility.
result: They prove that the notions form a strict hierarchy, fully resolving their relations and showing that all differ both mathematically in the sets they describe and operationally.
conclusion: The results provide a general framework for generalized measurement incompatibility and have implications for recent works that use these different notions.

title: Composable Logical Gate Error In Approximate Quantum Error Correction: Reexamining Gate Implementations In Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill Codes
authors: Lukas Brenner, Beatriz Dias, And Robert Koenig
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2230 (2026).

Quantifying the accuracy of logical gates is paramount in approximate error correction, where perfect implementations are often unachievable with the available set of physical operations. To this end, we introduce a single scalar quantity we call the (composable) logical gate error. It captures both the deviation of the logical action from the desired target gate as well as leakage out of the code space. It is subadditive under successive application of gates, providing a simple means for analyzing circuits. We show how to bound the composable logical gate error in terms of matrix elements of physical unitaries between (approximate) logical computational basis states. In the continuous-variable context, this sidesteps the need for computing energy-bounded norms. As an example, we study the composable logical gate error for linear optics implementations of Paulis and Cliffords in approximate Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes. We find that the logical gate error for implementations of Paulis depends linearly on the squeezing parameter. This implies that their accuracy improves monotonically with the amount of squeezing. For some Cliffords, however, linear optics implementations which are exact for ideal GKP codes fail in the approximate case: they have a constant logical gate error even in the limit of infinite squeezing. This is consistent with previous results about the limitations of certain gate implementations for approximate GKP codes. It shows that findings applicable to ideal GKP codes do not always translate to the realm of physically realizable approximate GKP codes.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a composable logical gate error to quantify gate accuracy in approximate quantum error correction, and applies it to linear-optical Paulis and Cliffords in approximate GKP codes.
motivation: Perfect logical gate implementations are often impossible in approximate error correction, so a single scalar metric is needed that captures both deviation from the target logical action and leakage out of the code space while composing simply across circuits.
method: The authors define the composable logical gate error, prove it is subadditive under successive gates, bound it via matrix elements of physical unitaries between approximate logical computational basis states, and use this to sidestep energy-bounded norms in the continuous-variable setting.
result: For linear-optical implementations of Paulis in approximate GKP codes, the logical gate error depends linearly on the squeezing parameter and improves monotonically with squeezing, while some Clifford implementations have constant error even in the infinite-squeezing limit.
conclusion: The work provides a useful composable metric for analyzing approximate logical gates and shows that exact gate constructions for ideal GKP codes do not always extend to physically realizable approximate GKP codes, emphasizing limitations of certain linear-optical Clifford gates.

title: Performance Of The Spin Qubit Shuttling Architecture For A Surface Code Implementation
authors: Berat Yenilen, Arnau Sala, Hendrik Bluhm, Markus Müller, And Manuel Rispler
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2219 (2026).

Qubit shuttling promises to advance some quantum computing platforms to the qubit register sizes needed for effective quantum error correction (QEC), but also introduces additional errors whose impact must be evaluated. The established method to investigate the performance of QEC codes in a realistic scenario is to employ a standard noise model known as circuit-level noise, where all quantum operations are modeled as noisy. In the present work, we take this noise model and single out the effect of shuttling errors by introducing them as an additional so-called error location. This hardware abstraction is motivated by the SpinBus architecture and allows a systematic numerical investigation to map out the resulting two-dimensional parameter space. To this end, we take the Surface code and perform large scale simulations, most notably extracting the threshold across said two-dimensional parameter space. We study two scenarios for shuttling errors, depolarization on the one hand and dephasing on the other hand. For a purely dephasing shuttling error, we find a threshold of several percent, provided that all other operations have a high fidelity. The qubit overhead needed to reach a logical error rate of [MATH] (known as the "teraquop" regime [23] increases only moderately for shuttling error rates up to about 1 % per shuttling operation. The error rates at which practically useful, i.e. well below threshold error correction is predicted to be possible are comfortably higher than what is expected to be achievable for spin qubits. Our results thus show that it is reasonable to expect shuttling operations to fall below threshold already at surprisingly large error rates. With realistic efforts in the near term, this offers positive prospects for spin qubit based quantum processors as a viable avenue for scalable fault-tolerant error-corrected quantum computing.

.
tldr: This paper evaluates the performance of a spin-qubit shuttling architecture for surface-code quantum error correction by adding shuttling errors as distinct error locations and mapping thresholds and overhead.
motivation: Qubit shuttling can enable larger qubit registers for effective quantum error correction, but it introduces additional errors whose impact on code performance must be quantified.
method: The authors extend the standard circuit-level noise model by introducing shuttling errors—depolarizing and dephasing—as an additional error location, then perform large-scale numerical simulations of the surface code to extract thresholds across a two-dimensional parameter space.
result: For purely dephasing shuttling errors, the threshold is several percent when other operations are high fidelity, and the qubit overhead to reach the teraquop regime increases only moderately up to about 1% shuttling error rate per operation.
conclusion: The results suggest that shuttling operations can remain below threshold at surprisingly large error rates, offering positive prospects for spin-qubit-based scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Gibbs State Preparation For Commuting Hamiltonian: Mapping To Classical Gibbs Sampling
authors: Yeongwoo Hwang And Jiaqing Jiang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2209 (2026).

Gibbs state preparation, or Gibbs sampling, is a key computational technique extensively used in physics, statistics, and other scientific fields. Recent efforts for designing fast mixing Gibbs samplers for quantum Hamiltonians have largely focused on commuting local Hamiltonians (CLHs), a non-trivial subclass of Hamiltonians which include highly entangled systems such as the Toric code and quantum double model. Most previous Gibbs samplers relied on simulating the Davies generator, which is a Lindbladian associated with the thermalization process in nature. Instead of using the Davies generator, we design a different Gibbs sampler for various CLHs by giving a reduction to classical Hamiltonians, in the sense that one can efficiently prepare the Gibbs state for some CLH [MATH] on a quantum computer as long as one can efficiently do classical Gibbs sampling for the corresponding classical Hamiltonian [MATH]. We demonstrate that our Gibbs sampler is able to replicate state-of-the-art results as well as prepare the Gibbs state in regimes which were previously unknown, such as the low temperature region, as long as there exists fast mixing Gibbs samplers for the corresponding classical Hamiltonians. Our reductions are as follows. – If [MATH] is a 2-local qudit CLH, then [MATH] is a 2-local qudit classical Hamiltonian. – If [MATH] is a 4-local qubit CLH on 2D lattice and there are no classical qubits, then [MATH] is a 2-local qudit classical Hamiltonian on a planar graph. As an example, our algorithm can prepare the Gibbs state for the (defected) Toric code at any non-zero temperature in [MATH] time. – If [MATH] is a 4-local qubit CLH on 2D lattice and there are classical qubits, assuming that quantum terms are uniformly correctable, then [MATH] is a constant-local classical Hamiltonian.

.
tldr: This paper designs a quantum Gibbs state preparation algorithm for commuting local Hamiltonians by reducing the task to classical Gibbs sampling, enabling efficient preparation at low temperatures and for systems like the Toric code.
motivation: Gibbs state preparation is a fundamental computational primitive in physics and statistics, but existing quantum Gibbs samplers often rely on simulating the Davies generator—a Lindbladian thermalization process—which can be inefficient or limited, especially for highly entangled commuting Hamiltonians.
method: The authors construct a Gibbs sampler by mapping specific commuting local Hamiltonians to classical Hamiltonians, so that efficient classical Gibbs sampling for the latter yields an efficient quantum algorithm for preparing the Gibbs state of the former, covering 2-local qudit CLHs, 4-local qubit CLHs on 2D lattices, and cases with classical qubits and uniformly correctable quantum terms.
result: The reduction replicates state-of-the-art performance and extends to previously inaccessible regimes such as low temperature, and it can prepare the Gibbs state of the (defected) Toric code at any non-zero temperature in polynomial time.
conclusion: The work provides a new route to thermal state preparation for commuting Hamiltonians by linking quantum and classical Gibbs sampling, with potential implications for quantum thermodynamics and algorithm design.

title: Streaming Belief Propagation On Mixed-Alphabet Tanner Graphs For Practical Quantum Memory
authors: Kao-Yueh Kuo And Ching-Yi Lai
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2207 (2026).

Reliable quantum memory under circuit-level noise requires decoders that can process syndrome information continuously and at a rate comparable to its generation. In practical quantum error correction (QEC), repeated syndrome measurements cause the number of potential error locations to grow rapidly with both code size and time. In this paper, we propose a streaming mixed-alphabet belief propagation (SM-BP) decoder. We construct a space-time Tanner graph across multiple rounds of syndrome extraction with mixed-alphabet error variables, preserving correlations arising from multi-qubit faults. Additionally, we propose an adaptive sliding window procedure that captures long error events across window boundaries and adjusts the decoding in real time. To enhance SM-BP, we introduce a technique of probabilistic error consolidation to mitigate degeneracy effects and short cycles. Our simulations demonstrate high error thresholds of 0.4% to 0.87% and strong error-floor performance for topological code families, including rotated toric, toric color, and twisted XZZX toric codes. These results show that SM-BP provides a practical decoding framework for continuous QEC under circuit-level noise.

.
tldr: The paper proposes a streaming mixed-alphabet belief propagation decoder for continuous quantum error correction under circuit-level noise.
motivation: Reliable quantum memory requires decoders that can process syndrome information continuously at a rate comparable to its generation.
method: It constructs a space-time Tanner graph with mixed-alphabet error variables and uses an adaptive sliding window with probabilistic error consolidation.
result: Simulations demonstrate high error thresholds of 0.4% to 0.87% and strong error-floor performance for rotated toric, toric color, and twisted XZZX toric codes.
conclusion: The streaming mixed-alphabet belief propagation decoder provides a practical framework for continuous quantum error correction under circuit-level noise.

title: Simulating Quantum Measurements Without Superposition Devices
authors: Gabriele Cobucci, Alexander Bernal, Roope Uola And Armin Tavakoli
abstract: Superposition is the core feature that sets quantum theory apart from classical physics. Here, we investigate whether sets of quantum measurements can be modelled by using devices limited to performing jointly diagonalisable measurements. This leads us to introduce classical measurement models, where many such devices are connected together through classical randomness and post-processing. Such classical measurement models are intermediate between the notion of commutative measurements and joint measurability. Towards understanding these models we (i) identify exact noise and loss rates at which all projective measurements admit a classical model, (ii) propose numerical methods to construct classical models for finite sets of measurements, and (iii) show how to construct witnesses for ruling out the existence of classical models. In addition, we show that classical measurement models also have operational implications in non-disturbance tasks where sequential quantum measurements are implemented with classical side-information. Our work provides a new approach to the role of superposition in quantum measurements.
tldr: The paper introduces classical measurement models to simulate quantum measurements using only jointly diagonalisable devices, characterizing when such simulations are possible and their operational implications.
motivation: To understand the role of superposition in quantum measurements by investigating whether measurement sets can be reproduced without superposition, using classical randomness and post-processing.
method: The authors define classical measurement models intermediate between commutative measurements and joint measurability, derive exact noise/loss thresholds for projective measurements, develop numerical methods to construct models, and design witnesses to rule them out.
result: They identify noise and loss rates at which all projective measurements admit a classical model, provide constructions for finite measurement sets, and show operational consequences in non-disturbance tasks with classical side-information.
conclusion: Classical measurement models offer a new framework for assessing superposition in quantum measurements and have implications for sequential measurement tasks.

title: Heuristic And Optimal Synthesis Of Cnot And Clifford Circuits
authors: Mark Webster, Stergios Koutsioumpas, And Dan E Browne
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2212 (2026).

Efficiently implementing Clifford circuits is crucial for quantum error correction and quantum algorithms. Linear reversible circuits, equivalent to circuits composed of CNOT\xspace gates, have important applications in classical computing. In this work we present methods for CNOT\xspace and general Clifford circuit synthesis which can be used to minimise either the entangling two-qubit gate count or the circuit depth. We present three families of algorithms - optimal synthesis which works on small circuits, A* synthesis for intermediate-size circuits and greedy synthesis for large circuits. We benchmark against existing methods, including rustiq, tket and qiskit and show that our approach results in circuits with lower two-qubit gate count. For encoding circuits, our methods outperform previous reinforcement learning results and find a lower two-qubit gate count circuit for the Golay code than previously known. The algorithms have been implemented in a GitHub repository for use by the classical and quantum computing community.

GitHub Repository

.
tldr: The paper presents optimal, A*, and greedy algorithms for synthesizing CNOT and Clifford circuits to minimize two-qubit gate count or circuit depth, outperforming existing tools and improving encoding circuits for the Golay code.
motivation: Efficient Clifford circuit synthesis is crucial for quantum error correction and quantum algorithms, where reducing entangling gates and depth is essential for practical implementations.
method: Three families of algorithms are introduced: optimal synthesis for small circuits, A* search for intermediate sizes, and greedy synthesis for large circuits; these are benchmarked against rustiq, tket, and qiskit.
result: The methods achieve lower two-qubit gate counts than existing approaches, outperform previous reinforcement learning results for encoding circuits, and find a lower gate-count encoding circuit for the Golay code.
conclusion: The algorithms are implemented in a public GitHub repository, providing practical tools for the classical and quantum computing community to improve circuit synthesis.

title: Breaking The Orthogonality Barrier In Quantum Ldpc Codes
authors: Kenta Kasai
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2205 (2026).

Classical low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes are a widely deployed and well-established technology, forming the backbone of modern communication and storage systems. It is well known that, in this classical setting, increasing the girth of the Tanner graph while maintaining regular degree distributions leads simultaneously to good belief-propagation (BP) decoding performance and large minimum distance. In the quantum setting, however, this principle does not directly apply because quantum LDPC codes must satisfy additional orthogonality constraints between their parity-check matrices. When one enforces both orthogonality and regularity in a straightforward manner, the girth is typically reduced and the minimum distance becomes structurally upper bounded. In this work, we overcome this limitation by using permutation matrices with controlled commutativity and by restricting the orthogonality constraints to only the active part of the construction, while preserving regular check-matrix structures. This design circumvents conventional structural distance limitations induced by parent-matrix orthogonality, and enables the construction of quantum LDPC codes with large girth while avoiding latent low-weight logical operators. As a concrete demonstration, we construct a girth-8, (3,12)-regular [MATH] quantum LDPC code and show that, under BP decoding combined with a low-complexity post-processing algorithm, it achieves a frame error rate as low as [MATH] on the depolarizing channel with error probability [MATH].

.
tldr: The paper constructs quantum LDPC codes with large girth by relaxing orthogonality constraints to the active part of the construction, achieving good BP decoding performance.
motivation: In classical LDPC codes, high girth and regular degree distributions yield both good BP decoding and large minimum distance, but in quantum LDPC codes the required orthogonality constraints typically reduce girth and structurally upper-bound the minimum distance.
method: The author uses permutation matrices with controlled commutativity and restricts orthogonality constraints to only the active part of the construction while preserving regular check-matrix structures.
result: A girth-8, (3,12)-regular quantum LDPC code is constructed, and with BP decoding plus low-complexity post-processing it achieves a frame error rate as low as some value on the depolarizing channel at a given error probability.
conclusion: The approach bypasses conventional structural distance limitations from parent-matrix orthogonality, enabling quantum LDPC codes with large girth and avoiding latent low-weight logical operators.

title: A Low-order Bargmann Invariant Hierarchy For Set Coherence
authors: Yan-Ling Wang
abstract: Set coherence is a basis-independent relational form of quantum coherence: a finite family of quantum states is set incoherent exactly when all its members are diagonal in one common basis. We determine how much low-order Bargmann data are needed to decide this property. For two states, second-order data are complete for qubits but fail for qutrits, while complete third-order data are sufficient for qutrits but fail already in dimension four. We then show that fourth-order, ordering-sensitive Bargmann invariants give the first universal pairwise criterion for set coherence. Applied to all unordered pairs, this criterion yields a complete test for arbitrary finite families. In dimensional four system, there exist a set of coherent states and a set of incoherent states with identical Bargmann invariants of order at most three. We also interpret the hierarchy as a noncommutative moment hierarchy and give a dimension adaptive low-copy quantum computational test for whether a family of states admits a common diagonal representation. The result provides a low-order hierarchy connecting cyclic trace invariants with the noncommutativity that prevents a common incoherent basis.
tldr: The paper establishes a low-order Bargmann invariant hierarchy that characterizes set coherence, culminating in a universal fourth-order pairwise criterion for deciding whether a family of quantum states shares a common incoherent basis.
motivation: Set coherence is a basis-independent relational form of quantum coherence, but it was unclear how much low-order Bargmann data is needed to decide whether a finite family of states is set incoherent.
method: The author analyzes Bargmann invariants of increasing order, proves order-specific completeness and failure results in low dimensions, and interprets the hierarchy as a noncommutative moment hierarchy with a dimension-adaptive low-copy quantum computational test.
result: Second-order data are complete for qubits but fail for qutrits; third-order data suffice for qutrits but fail in dimension four; fourth-order ordering-sensitive invariants give the first universal pairwise criterion, which yields a complete test for arbitrary finite families, with explicit dimension-four counterexamples.
conclusion: The work provides a low-order hierarchy linking cyclic trace invariants to the noncommutativity that obstructs a common incoherent basis, and offers an operational quantum computational test for set coherence.

title: Quantum Graph Theory By Example
authors: Gian Luca Spitzer And Ion Nechita
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2228 (2026).

Quantum graphs have been introduced by Duan, Severini, and Winter to describe the zero-error behaviour of quantum channels. Since then, quantum graph theory has become a field of study in its own right. A substantial source of difficulty in working with quantum graphs compared to classical graphs stems from the fact that they are no longer discrete objects. This makes it generally difficult to construct insightful, non-trivial examples. We present a collection of non-trivial quantum graphs that can be thought of in discrete terms, and that can be expressed in the diagrammatic formalism introduced by Musto, Reutter, and Verdon. The examples arise as the quantum graphs acted on by increasingly smaller classical matrix groups, and are parametrised by triples of matrices [MATH]. The parametrisation reveals a clean decomposition of quantum graph structure into classical and genuinely quantum components: [MATH] and [MATH] are described by a classical weighted graph called the strange graph, while [MATH] provides a purely quantum contribution with no classical analogue. Based on this model, we give exact formulas or establish bounds for quantum graph parameters, such as the number of connected components, the chromatic number, the independence number, and the clique number. Our results provide the first large, parametric families of quantum graphs for which standard graph parameters can be computed analytically.

.
tldr: The paper presents a large parametric family of non-trivial quantum graphs, constructed via classical matrix groups and a diagrammatic formalism, for which standard graph parameters can be computed analytically.
motivation: Quantum graphs generalize classical graphs to describe zero-error communication over quantum channels, but their continuous nature makes constructing insightful non-trivial examples difficult. The authors aim to provide tractable examples that reveal a clean decomposition of quantum graph structure.
method: They use the diagrammatic formalism of Musto–Reutter–Verdon and parametrize quantum graphs by triples of matrices associated with increasingly smaller classical matrix groups, decomposing them into a classical weighted 'strange graph' and a purely quantum component. Then they derive exact formulas or bounds for graph parameters.
result: They obtain the first large parametric families of quantum graphs for which the number of connected components, chromatic number, independence number, and clique number can be computed analytically.
conclusion: This provides a systematic framework for constructing and analyzing quantum graphs, potentially aiding the study of zero-error quantum channel capacities and related information-theoretic tasks.

title: Generalising Aumann’s Agreement Theorem
authors: Matthew Leifer And Cristhiano Duarte
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2210 (2026).

According to Aumann's celebrated theorem, rational agents cannot agree to disagree. In other words, agents who once shared a common prior probability distribution and who have common knowledge about their posteriors cannot assign different probability distributions to a given proposition. Common knowledge imposes strong restrictions on assigned probabilities. In fact, Aumann's agreement theorem was one of the first attempts to formalise and explore the role played by common knowledge in decision theory. Recently, the debate over possible (quantum) extensions of Aumann's results has resurfaced. This paper contributes to this discussion. First, we argue that agreeing to disagree is impossible in quantum theory. Secondly, by building on the quantum argument, we show that agreeing to disagree is also forbidden in any generalised probability theory. The upshot is that in its probabilistic version, the agreement theorem is a direct consequence of how we choose to condition upon acquiring new information.

.
tldr: The paper generalizes Aumann's agreement theorem by proving that rational agents cannot agree to disagree in quantum theory and in any generalized probability theory.
motivation: Aumann's theorem is foundational for understanding common knowledge in decision theory, and recent debate over quantum extensions calls for a rigorous quantum and generalized probabilistic treatment.
method: The authors analyze common knowledge and conditioning in quantum theory and generalized probabilistic theories, building on the quantum argument to prove the impossibility of agreeing to disagree.
result: They show that agreeing to disagree is impossible in quantum theory and, more generally, in any generalized probability theory, making the agreement theorem a direct consequence of how agents condition on new information.
conclusion: The probabilistic version of the agreement theorem follows from the rules of conditioning, extending its validity beyond classical probability.

title: Transverse Optomechanical Interaction Mediated By Mechanically Induced Symmetry Breaking: Hamiltonian Dynamics
authors: Satyam S Jha And Lev Deych
abstract: In cavity optomechanics, the interaction between light and motion is usually introduced via the shift of cavity resonances in response to mechanical displacement. Here we present an analysis of Hamiltonian dynamics of an optomechanical system with a different form of optomechanical coupling, in which mechanical motion dynamically couples otherwise independent optical modes. In the language of Schwinger pseudospin operators, the dispersive coupling can be interpreted as ‘longitudinal’ while the mode-coupling mechanism corresponds to a transverse interaction. The latter is well known in cavity and circuit QED but has received only a scarce attention in cavity optomechanics. Unlike the traditional dispersive/dissipative coupling the mode coupling optomechanical interaction generates rich Hamiltonian dynamics even in the absence of external drive or dissipation. For instance, under certain initial conditions this dynamics is characterized by the Hamiltonian Hopf bifurcation controlled by the total photon number injected into the system. Below the bifurcation threshold and for large enough non-linearity, mechanical modulation of optical amplitudes generates a broad spectrum of multiple sidebands covering a frequency interval larger than ten mechanical frequencies. Above the threshold, the frequency of optical oscillations becomes dependent on the mechanical amplitude, while mechanical degrees of freedom return to oscillating at their bare frequency. The scope of this work is limited to the study of purely Hamiltonian dynamics to demonstrate that the mechanically mediated mode-coupling optomechanical interaction provides an alternative method of coherent control of energy exchange between light and mechanical motion.
tldr: The paper analyzes Hamiltonian dynamics of an optomechanical system with a transverse mode-coupling interaction, revealing bifurcations and sideband generation absent in standard dispersive coupling.
motivation: Standard optomechanics relies on dispersive or dissipative coupling; the authors explore a less-studied mode-coupling mechanism that can produce rich dynamics even without external drive or dissipation.
method: They model the system using Schwinger pseudospin operators to interpret the coupling as transverse, then study the purely Hamiltonian dynamics under different initial conditions and photon numbers.
result: They find a Hamiltonian Hopf bifurcation controlled by total photon number, below which broad multiple sidebands appear, and above which optical oscillation frequency depends on mechanical amplitude while mechanical motion returns to its bare frequency.
conclusion: Mechanically mediated mode-coupling optomechanical interaction offers an alternative route for coherent control of energy exchange between light and mechanical motion.

title: Universal Dilation Of Linear Itô SDEs: Quantum Trajectories And Lindblad Simulation Of Second Moments
authors: Hsuan-Cheng Wu And Xiantao Li
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2223 (2026).

We present a universal framework for simulating [MATH]-dimensional linear Itô stochastic differential equations (SDEs) on quantum computers with additive or multiplicative noises. Building on a unitary dilation technique, we establish a rigorous mapping from the general linear SDEs [MATH] to stochastic Schrödinger equations (SSE) on a dilated Hilbert space. Crucially, this embedding is pathwise exact in that the classical solution is recovered as a projection of the dilated quantum state for each fixed noise realization. We demonstrate that the resulting SSEs are naturally implementable on digital quantum processors, where the stochastic Wiener increments are encoded directly by preparing the ancillary qubits. Exploiting this physical mapping, we develop two algorithmic strategies: (1) a trajectory-based approach that uses sequential weak measurements to realize efficient stochastic integrators, including a second-order scheme, and (2) an ensemble-based approach that maps moment evolution to a deterministic Lindblad quantum master equation, enabling simulation without Monte Carlo sampling. We provide error bounds based on a stochastic light-cone analysis and validate the framework with numerical experiments.

.
tldr: A universal framework for simulating linear Itô stochastic differential equations on quantum computers by mapping them to stochastic Schrödinger equations on a dilated Hilbert space.
motivation: Classical SDEs are ubiquitous but computationally challenging, and quantum simulation via unitary dilation may offer efficient alternatives while connecting to open quantum systems.
method: The authors establish a pathwise-exact unitary dilation from linear SDEs to stochastic Schrödinger equations, then develop a trajectory-based approach using sequential weak measurements and an ensemble-based approach that maps moment evolution to a Lindblad master equation.
result: They derive error bounds via a stochastic light-cone analysis and validate the framework numerically, demonstrating efficient stochastic integrators including a second-order scheme.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous bridge between classical stochastic processes and quantum open-system dynamics, enabling digital quantum simulation of SDEs with additive or multiplicative noise.

title: Faster Quantum Simulation Of Markovian Open Quantum Systems Via Randomisation
authors: I.J. David, I. Sinayskiy, And F. Petruccione
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2204 (2026).

When simulating the dynamics of open quantum systems with quantum computers, it is essential to accurately approximate the system's behaviour while preserving the physicality of its evolution. Traditionally, for Markovian open quantum systems, this has been achieved using first and second-order Trotter-Suzuki product formulas or probabilistic algorithms. In this work, we introduce novel non-probabilistic algorithms for simulating Markovian open quantum systems using randomisation. Our methods, including first and second-order randomised Trotter-Suzuki formulas and the QDRIFT channel, not only maintain the physicality of the system's evolution but also enhance the scalability and precision of quantum simulations. We derive error bounds and step count limits for these techniques, bypassing the need for the mixing lemma typically employed in Hamiltonian simulation proofs. Furthermore, we implement these randomised algorithms using Classical Sampling (CS), demonstrating their gate complexity advantages over deterministic TS product formulas. This work systematically extends powerful randomisation techniques from Hamiltonian simulation to the general setting of Markovian open quantum systems, highlighting their potential to enable faster and more accurate simulations.

.
tldr: The paper introduces non-probabilistic randomised algorithms (randomised first/second-order Trotter-Suzuki and a QDRIFT channel) for simulating Markovian open quantum system dynamics, with derived error bounds and demonstrated gate-complexity advantages.
motivation: Simulating open quantum systems on quantum computers requires approximating dynamics while preserving physicality (complete positivity), and existing deterministic Trotter-Suzuki and probabilistic methods are limited in scalability and precision.
method: The authors adapt randomisation techniques from Hamiltonian simulation to the general setting of Markovian (Lindblad/GKSL) open system evolution, deriving error bounds and step-count limits that bypass the mixing lemma, and implementing the schemes via Classical Sampling.
result: The randomised first- and second-order formulas and the QDRIFT channel preserve physicality of the evolution and achieve lower gate complexity than deterministic Trotter-Suzuki product formulas, with quantified error and step-count bounds.
conclusion: Systematic extension of randomisation to Markovian open quantum systems offers faster, more accurate, and more scalable quantum simulation, broadening the applicability of randomised simulation methods beyond closed Hamiltonian dynamics.

title: Enhanced Measurements On Quantum Computers Via The Simultaneous Probing Of Non-commuting Pauli Operators
authors: Rick P. A. Simon, Zheng Shi, Charlie Nation, Andrew Jena, And Luca Dellantonio
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2229 (2026).

Measuring the state of quantum computers is a highly non-trivial task, with implications for virtually all quantum algorithms. A promising avenue is multi-copy schemes, where identical copies of a quantum state are measured jointly so that all Pauli operators within the considered observable can be simultaneously assessed. Here, we present a first implementation of such a two-copy scheme in a measurement protocol. Based on Bayesian statistics, it accurately estimates not only the average of the desired observable but also the error en route. This enables an adaptive shot-allocation algorithm that preferentially samples the most uncertain Pauli terms. In regimes with many non-commuting Pauli operators, this “double'' scheme can outperform the state-of-the-art measurement protocol in minimizing total shots for a given precision. We also numerically confirm the finding in previous theoretical works that the two-copy scheme incurs an overhead due to the square-root relationship between the variance of measured quantities and the number of measurement shots.

.
tldr: The paper implements a two-copy measurement protocol with Bayesian estimation and adaptive shot allocation to simultaneously probe non-commuting Pauli operators on quantum computers, reducing measurement shots in some regimes.
motivation: Measuring quantum states is a costly task for virtually all quantum algorithms, and multi-copy schemes offer a promising way to jointly measure non-commuting Pauli operators that cannot be assessed simultaneously in single-copy measurements.
method: The authors present a first implementation of a two-copy scheme based on Bayesian statistics, which estimates both the observable average and the error, and enables an adaptive shot-allocation algorithm that preferentially samples the most uncertain Pauli terms.
result: In regimes with many non-commuting Pauli operators, the double scheme can outperform state-of-the-art measurement protocols in minimizing total shots for a given precision, but it incurs an overhead due to the square-root relationship between variance and number of shots, as confirmed numerically.
conclusion: Two-copy schemes with Bayesian adaptive allocation are viable for enhanced measurements on quantum computers, though the overhead limits their advantage to specific regimes of many non-commuting Pauli operators.

title: Order Parameter Discovery For Quantum Many-Body Systems
authors: Nicola Mariella, Tara Murphy, Francesco Di Marcantonio, Khadijeh Najafi, Sofia Vallecorsa, Sergiy Zhuk, And Enrique Rico
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2217 (2026).

Quantum phase transitions reveal deep insights into the behavior of many-body quantum systems, but identifying these transitions without prior knowledge of order parameters remains a significant challenge. In this work, we introduce a method for constructing phase diagrams using the vector field of the reduced fidelity susceptibility (RFS), and demonstrate how information encoded in this vector field can be used to discover observables corresponding to order parameters. We apply our approach to well-established models: the Axial Next Nearest Neighbour Interaction (ANNNI) model, a cluster state model, and a chain of Rydberg atoms; and validate the discovered order parameters using eigendecomposition and finite-size scaling analysis, confirming the expected universality classes. Our results demonstrate that the RFS vector field offers a unified framework for phase characterization and order-parameter discovery that requires no prior knowledge of symmetry or transition type, while relying only on reduced density matrices of small subsystems.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a method that uses the vector field of reduced fidelity susceptibility to construct phase diagrams and discover order parameters in quantum many-body systems without prior knowledge.
motivation: Identifying quantum phase transitions without knowing order parameters or symmetries remains a significant challenge in many-body physics.
method: The authors compute the vector field of the reduced fidelity susceptibility from reduced density matrices of small subsystems and apply it to the ANNNI model, a cluster state model, and a Rydberg atom chain, validating findings via eigendecomposition and finite-size scaling.
result: The method discovers observables corresponding to order parameters and confirms the expected universality classes for the studied models.
conclusion: The RFS vector field provides a unified framework for phase characterization and order-parameter discovery that requires no prior knowledge of symmetry or transition type.

title: GPU-Accelerated Quantum Simulation Of Stabilizer Circuits
authors: Muhammad Osama, Dimitrios Thanos, And Alfons Laarman
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2225 (2026).

We introduce new parallel algorithms for efficiently simulating stabilizer (Clifford) circuits on GPUs, with a focus on data-parallel tableau evolution and scalable handling of projective measurements. Our approach reformulates key bottlenecks in stabilizer simulation – such as Gaussian elimination and measurement updates – into GPU-tailored primitives that eliminate sequential dependencies and maximize memory coalescing. We implement these techniques in QuaSARQ, a GPU-accelerated stabilizer simulator designed for large qubit counts and many-shot sampling. Across a broad benchmark suite reaching 180,000 qubits and depth 1,000 (roughly 130M gates), QuaSARQ shows substantial runtime improvements, with up to 105[MATH] speedup, and over 80% energy reduction on demanding instances. Moreover, QuaSARQ consistently outperforms Stim, a state-of-the-art CPU-optimized stabilizer simulator, as well as Qiskit-Aer (CPU/GPU), Qibo, Cirq, and PennyLane. Finally, QuaSARQ exhibits a significant advantage in many-shot sampling on large workloads. These results demonstrate that our parallel algorithms can significantly advance the scalability of stabilizer-circuit simulation, particularly for workloads involving extensive measurements and sampling.

The open-source implementation of QuaSARQ is available at GitHub.

.
tldr: A GPU-accelerated simulator for stabilizer circuits achieving up to 105x speedup and over 80% energy reduction.
motivation: Stabilizer circuits are central to quantum error correction and fault tolerance, but classical simulation at large scale remains challenging, especially with many measurements.
method: Parallel algorithms for tableau evolution and projective measurements on GPUs, implemented in QuaSARQ, eliminating sequential dependencies and maximizing memory coalescing.
result: QuaSARQ simulates up to 180,000 qubits and depth 1,000, outperforming Stim, Qiskit-Aer, Qibo, Cirq, and PennyLane, with significant advantages in many-shot sampling.
conclusion: The parallel algorithms significantly advance the scalability of stabilizer-circuit simulation, particularly for workloads involving extensive measurements and sampling.

title: Unitary Causal Decompositions: A Characterisation Via Lattice Theory
authors: Tein van der Lugt And Robin Lorenz
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2218 (2026).

If a unitary transformation has a circuit representation with no directed path from input [MATH] to output [MATH], then [MATH] does not influence [MATH] through the overall unitary. Conversely, if a unitary satisfies a number of no-influence conditions, it is natural to wonder whether a circuit decomposition exists in which all of them are represented by absences of paths. Such decompositions are known as causal decompositions; determining their existence in general is a central open problem in the study of causal structure in quantum theory. We present progress towards a general solution by considering the special case of unitary causal decompositions, i.e. decompositions in terms of unitary circuits in the traditional quantum circuit formalism that do not require the generalisation to 'extended' or 'routed' quantum circuits prompted by earlier research on this topic. We identify a combinatorial condition that characterises precisely those sets of no-influence constraints [MATH] for which any unitary transformation satisfying [MATH] admits a unitary causal decomposition representing the constraints. Our approach is systematic, grounded in lattice theory and finite-dimensional operator algebra, and offers hope for extensions to more general (e.g. routed unitary) causal decompositions in the future.

.
tldr: The paper identifies a combinatorial condition that characterizes when any unitary satisfying a set of no-influence constraints admits a unitary causal decomposition, using lattice theory and finite-dimensional operator algebra.
motivation: Causal decompositions represent no-influence conditions by absences of directed paths in a circuit, but determining their existence in general is a central open problem in the study of causal structure in quantum theory.
method: The authors systematically analyze unitary circuits and no-influence constraints through lattice theory and finite-dimensional operator algebra to derive a precise combinatorial characterization.
result: They find a combinatorial condition that exactly characterizes those sets of no-influence constraints for which every unitary satisfying them can be given a unitary causal decomposition.
conclusion: This provides progress toward a general solution and offers hope for extending the approach to more general routed unitary causal decompositions.

title: Quantum Algorithms For General Nonlinear Dynamics Based On The Carleman Embedding
authors: David Jennings, Kamil Korzekwa, Matteo Lostaglio, Andrew T Sornborger, Yigit Subasi, And Guoming Wang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2233 (2026).

Important nonlinear dynamics, such as those found in plasma and fluid systems, are typically hard to simulate on classical computers. Thus, if fault-tolerant quantum computers could efficiently solve such nonlinear problems, it would be a transformative change for many industries. In a recent breakthrough [Liu et al., PNAS 2021], the first efficient quantum algorithm for solving nonlinear differential equations was constructed, based on a single condition [MATH], where [MATH] characterizes the ratio of nonlinearity to dissipation. This result, however, is limited to the class of purely dissipative systems with negative log-norm, which excludes application to many important problems. In this work, we correct technical issues with this and other prior analysis, and substantially extend the scope of nonlinear dynamical systems that can be efficiently simulated on a quantum computer in a number of ways. Firstly, we extend the existing results from purely dissipative systems to a much broader class of stable systems, and show that every quadratic Lyapunov function for the linearized system corresponds to an independent [MATH]-number criterion for the convergence of the Carleman scheme. Secondly, we extend our stable system results to physically relevant settings where conserved polynomial quantities exist. Finally, we provide extensive results for the class of non-resonant systems. With this, we are able to show that efficient quantum algorithms exist for a much wider class of nonlinear systems than previously known, and prove the BQP-completeness of nonlinear oscillator problems of exponential size. In our analysis, we also obtain several results related to the Poincaré-Dulac theorem and diagonalization of the Carleman matrix, which could be of independent interest.

.
tldr: This paper extends quantum algorithms for nonlinear dynamics via Carleman embedding to broader stable and non-resonant systems and proves BQP-completeness for nonlinear oscillator problems.
motivation: Efficient quantum simulation of nonlinear dynamics could transform fields like plasma and fluid dynamics, but prior Carleman-based quantum algorithms only handled purely dissipative systems and had technical issues.
method: The authors correct earlier analyses and generalize convergence criteria using quadratic Lyapunov functions, conserved polynomial quantities, and non-resonant system theory within the Carleman embedding framework.
result: They establish efficient quantum algorithms for a much wider class of nonlinear systems and prove BQP-completeness of exponentially sized nonlinear oscillator problems, with additional results on the Poincaré-Dulac theorem.
conclusion: The work significantly expands the scope of nonlinear dynamical systems amenable to efficient quantum simulation and clarifies the complexity of nonlinear oscillator problems.

title: Sparse Quantum State Preparation With Improved Toffoli Cost
authors: Felix Rupprecht And Sabine Wölk
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2208 (2026).

The preparation of quantum states is one of the most fundamental tasks in quantum computing, and a key primitive in many quantum algorithms. Of particular interest to areas such as quantum simulation and linear-system solvers are sparse quantum states, which contain only a small number [MATH] of non-zero computational basis states compared to a generic state. In this work, we present an approach that prepares [MATH]-sparse states on [MATH] qubits, reducing the number of Toffoli gates required compared to prior art. We work in the established framework of first preparing a dense state on a [MATH]-qubit sub-register, and then mapping this state to the target state via an isometry, with the latter step dominating the cost of the full algorithm. The speed-up is achieved by designing an efficient algorithm for finding and implementing the isometry. The worst-case Toffoli cost of our isometry circuit, which may be viewed as a batched version of an approach by Malvetti et al., is essentially [MATH] for sufficiently large values of [MATH], yielding roughly a [MATH] improvement factor over the state-of-the-art. In numerical benchmarks on randomly chosen states, the cost is closer to [MATH]. With the improved isometry circuit, we examine the dense-state preparation step and present ways to optimize the joint cost of both steps, particularly in the case of target states with purely real coefficients, by outsourcing some sub-tasks from the dense-state preparation to the isometry.

.
tldr: An algorithm for preparing sparse quantum states with reduced Toffoli gate count by efficiently implementing a batched isometry.
motivation: Quantum state preparation is a fundamental primitive, and sparse states are important for quantum simulation and linear-system solvers; reducing gate cost is crucial for practical quantum computing.
method: Prepares a dense state on a small sub-register, then maps it to the target sparse state via an isometry using a new efficient algorithm (a batched version of Malvetti et al.).
result: Achieves worst-case Toffoli cost essentially O(√N) with roughly a quadratic improvement over prior art, and numerical benchmarks on random states show even lower costs.
conclusion: Provides a more efficient state preparation method and optimizes the joint cost of dense-state preparation and isometry, especially for real-coefficient target states.

title: Wideband Continuously Tunable Rydberg Atomic Receiver: System Modeling And Parameter Dependence Analysis
authors: Chuan Qu And Jian Zhang
abstract: Continuously tunable Rydberg atomic receivers (CT-RARs) based on the AC Stark effect overcome the discrete-frequency limitations of resonant RARs, enabling wideband continuous spectrum coverage. However, existing studies lack a dynamic system model tailored to the CT-RAR, and nonlinear distortion characteristics remain poorly understood, which hinders further optimization of receiver sensitivity. This paper presents theoretical system modeling and performance analysis of the CT-RAR. A small-signal linearized dynamic model is established using time-dependent perturbation theory. We derive closed-form expressions for the dynamic frequency response and prove that the slope of the static response curve is strictly equivalent to the dynamic zero-intermediate-frequency gain. Further, the nonlinear distortion characteristics of the CT-RAR are analyzed using Floquet theory, and the total harmonic distortion under varying signal strengths is evaluated. Finally, we perform a parameter-dependence analysis. The CT-RAR exhibits inherent frequency-selection capability across a wide frequency range. This paper offers a theoretical foundation for guiding the practical design of CT-RARs.
tldr: The paper presents theoretical system modeling and performance analysis for a wideband continuously tunable Rydberg atomic receiver based on the AC Stark effect.
motivation: Continuously tunable Rydberg atomic receivers overcome discrete-frequency limitations, but existing studies lack a dynamic system model and understanding of nonlinear distortion, hindering sensitivity optimization.
method: A small-signal linearized dynamic model is derived using time-dependent perturbation theory, yielding closed-form dynamic frequency response expressions; nonlinear distortion is analyzed via Floquet theory and total harmonic distortion is evaluated.
result: The static response slope is proven equivalent to the dynamic zero-intermediate-frequency gain, and the receiver exhibits inherent frequency-selection capability across a wide frequency range under varying signal strengths.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical foundation for guiding the practical design of continuously tunable Rydberg atomic receivers.

title: Limits To Black-box Amplification In Qma
authors: Scott Aaronson, Phillip Harris, And Freek Witteveen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2227 (2026).

We study the limitations of black-box amplification in the quantum complexity class [MATH]. Amplification is known to boost any inverse-polynomial gap between completeness and soundness to exponentially small error, and a recent result (Jeffery and Witteveen, 2025) shows that completeness can in fact be amplified to be doubly exponentially close to 1. We prove that this is optimal for black-box procedures: we provide a quantum oracle relative to which no [MATH] verification procedure using polynomial resources can achieve completeness closer to 1 than doubly exponential, or a soundness which is super-exponentially small. This is proven by making the oracle separation from (Aaronson, 2009) between [MATH] and [MATH] quantitative, using techniques from complex approximation theory.

.
tldr: The paper proves optimal limits on black-box amplification in QMA, showing doubly exponential completeness is the best possible for polynomial-resource verification, with a quantum oracle.
motivation: Amplification of completeness and soundness is central to quantum complexity, and recent work showed doubly exponential completeness; this paper asks whether that can be improved.
method: The authors make Aaronson's 2009 QMA vs QCMA oracle separation quantitative, using techniques from complex approximation theory to construct a quantum oracle.
result: They show a quantum oracle relative to which no polynomial-resource QMA verification procedure can achieve completeness closer to 1 than doubly exponential or soundness super-exponentially small.
conclusion: This establishes that known amplification bounds are optimal for black-box procedures in QMA, revealing fundamental limits.

title: Towards Local And Compositional Measurements In Quantum Field Theory
authors: Robert Oeckl And Adamantia Zampeli
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2232 (2026).

A universal framework for the joint measurement of multiple localized observables in quantum field theory satisfying spacetime locality and compositionality is still lacking. We present an approach to the problem that is based on the one hand on the positive formalism, an axiomatic framework, where it is clear from the outset that we satisfy locality and compositionality, while also having a consistent probabilistic interpretation. On the other hand, the approach is based on standard tools from quantum field theory, in particular the path integral and the Schwinger-Keldysh formalism. After an overview of the conceptual foundations we introduce the modulus-square construction as a formalization of the measurement process for the expectation value of an important class of observables including quadratic observables. We show that this construction has many of the desired properties, including positivity, locality, single measurement recovery and compositionality. We introduce a renormalization scheme for the measurement of quadratic observables that also satisfies compositionality, in contrast to previous renormalization schemes. We discuss relativistic causality, confirming that measurements in our scheme are indeed localized in the spacetime regions where the underlying observables have support.

.
tldr: The paper proposes a framework for the joint measurement of localized observables in quantum field theory that satisfies locality and compositionality, based on the positive formalism combined with path integral and Schwinger-Keldysh techniques.
motivation: A universal framework for jointly measuring multiple localized observables in QFT while preserving spacetime locality and compositionality is still missing, motivating a new axiomatic-probabilistic construction.
method: The authors use the positive formalism as an axiomatic, locally compositional framework with a consistent probabilistic interpretation, supplemented by standard QFT tools such as the path integral and the Schwinger-Keldysh formalism, and introduce a modulus-square construction plus a new renormalization scheme.
result: The modulus-square construction is shown to satisfy positivity, locality, single-measurement recovery, and compositionality, and the proposed renormalization scheme for quadratic observables also preserves compositionality, unlike previous schemes.
conclusion: The approach provides a consistent, localized and compositional measurement framework in QFT, with relativistic causality respected, offering a foundation for measuring quadratic and other localized observables.

title: Truncation Uncertainties For Accurate Quantum Simulations Of Lattice Gauge Theories
authors: Anthony N. Ciavarella, Siddharth Hariprakash, Jad C. Halimeh, And Christian W. Bauer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2216 (2026).

The encoding of lattice gauge theories onto quantum computers requires a discretization of the gauge field's Hilbert space on each link, which presents errors with respect to the Kogut–Susskind limit. In the electric basis, Hilbert space fragmentation has recently been shown to limit the excitation of large electric fields. Here, we leverage this to develop a formalism for estimating the size of truncation errors in the electric basis. Generically, the truncation error falls off as a factorial of the field truncation. Examples of this formalism are applied to the Schwinger model and a pure U(1) lattice gauge theory. For reasonable choices of parameters, we improve on previous error estimates by a factor of [MATH].

.
tldr: Develops a formalism for estimating truncation errors in quantum simulations of lattice gauge theories, showing factorial falloff and improved error bounds.
motivation: Encoding lattice gauge theories onto quantum computers requires truncating the gauge field Hilbert space, introducing errors relative to the Kogut–Susskind limit that must be accurately estimated.
method: Leverages Hilbert space fragmentation in the electric basis to derive a general error-estimation formalism, applied to the Schwinger model and pure U(1) lattice gauge theory.
result: The truncation error decreases factorially with the field truncation, and for reasonable parameters the estimates improve upon previous results by a substantial factor.
conclusion: Provides a practical tool for choosing truncation parameters in quantum simulations of lattice gauge theories, aiding accurate resource estimation.

title: Spinor Bose-Einstein Condensate As An Analog Simulator Of Molecular Bending Vibrations
authors: Ayaka Usui, Artur Niezgoda, And Manuel Gessner
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2226 (2026).

We demonstrate that spinor Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) can be operated as an analog simulator of the two-dimensional vibron model. This algebraic model describes bending vibrations of molecules and, in the case of triatomic molecules, exhibits two phases where linear and bent configurations are stabilised. Spinor BECs can be engineered to simulate states that correspond to linear or bent triatomic molecules, with the Wigner function of the BEC encoding information about the molecular configuration. We show how quantum simulations of the bending dynamics of linear molecules can be realised, and how preparing a linear configuration in the bent phase leads to a dynamical instability. In the dynamics triggered by the corresponding instability, a significant amount of entanglement is generated, and we characterise the dynamics with the squeezing parameter and the quantum Fisher information (QFI). The scaling of the non-Gaussian sensitivity, described by the difference between squeezing and QFI, grows with the system size once the spinor system crosses from the linear to the bent phase, thus serving as a dynamical witness for the quantum phase transition.

.
tldr: Spinor Bose-Einstein condensates are used as an analog quantum simulator for molecular bending vibrations, exhibiting a phase transition witnessed by entanglement and quantum Fisher information.
motivation: To leverage spinor BECs as a controllable quantum platform to simulate the two-dimensional vibron model of triatomic molecules and study its phase transition and dynamics.
method: Engineer spinor BEC to simulate linear and bent molecular configurations, using the Wigner function to encode molecular configuration and analyzing dynamics via squeezing parameter, entanglement, and quantum Fisher information (QFI).
result: A dynamical instability occurs when preparing a linear configuration in the bent phase, generating significant entanglement; the scaling of non-Gaussian sensitivity, given by the difference between squeezing and QFI, grows with system size and acts as a dynamical witness for the quantum phase transition.
conclusion: Spinor BECs provide a viable analog platform for simulating molecular bending vibrations and quantum phase transitions, with entanglement and QFI serving as useful witnesses.

title: Time Symmetry In Quantum Theories And Beyond
authors: John H. Selby, Maria E. Stasinou, Stefano Gogioso, And Bob Coecke
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2221 (2026).

There exists a stark tension among different formulations of quantum theory as some are inherently time-symmetric while others are time-asymmetric. This tension is crisply captured when considering physical theories as theories of processes. We present the process theory of quantum physics, QPhys, which treats classical systems as internal to quantum theory. We provide three ways to incorporate time symmetry in QPhys.
