The first restricts the process theory of QPhys to one that satisfies an additional retrocausality constraint. The second is a novel approach, which extends the notions of causality and retrocausality to apply to systems along with processes. Utilizing this approach, we create a toy model for particle physics , where the causal and retrocausal systems correspond to particles and anti-particles respectively. The third approach extends QPhys to a supertheory that satisfies neither a causality nor a retrocausality constraint. To avoid unphysical predictions we modify either its composition rule or its processes.

.
tldr: The paper presents the process theory QPhys and three ways to incorporate time symmetry, including a retrocausal constraint and a toy particle physics model.
motivation: There is a stark tension between time-symmetric and time-asymmetric formulations of quantum theory, which is crisply captured when considering physical theories as theories of processes.
method: The authors introduce QPhys, then modify it by (i) adding a retrocausality constraint, (ii) extending causality and retrocausality to systems as well as processes, and (iii) extending QPhys to a supertheory with neither constraint.
result: The system-level approach yields a toy model where causal and retrocausal systems correspond to particles and antiparticles, while the supertheory avoids unphysical predictions by modifying composition or processes.
conclusion: The work offers new process-theoretic perspectives on time symmetry in quantum theories and beyond, with potential applications to particle physics models.

title: Evidence For Exceptional Points As Topological Defects
authors: Chia-Yi Ju And Szu-Ming Chen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2220 (2026).

Studies have shown that quantum states reside in a Hilbert space bundle. When a quantum system depends on continuous external parameters, these parameters define additional dimensions in the base space of the bundle. While much of the existing literature focuses on eigenstate subbundles, where geometric properties like Berry curvature arise, this work considers the entire Hilbert space bundle. Although the Hilbert space bundle has been found to be locally flat, suggesting that the system's topology may appear trivial, we revisit this assumption. Specifically, we examine how an arbitrary quantum state evolves when transported along closed parameter loops, a phenomenon characterized by holonomy. Our results demonstrate that nontrivial holonomy can emerge in the presence of exceptional points. Consequently, exceptional points naturally manifest as topological defects. Finally, we show that this nontrivial topology manifests in physical, time-dependent evolutions, providing a simple experimental signature to detect exceptional points by comparing state transport along distinct paths.

.
tldr: The paper shows that exceptional points act as topological defects in the Hilbert space bundle, detectable via nontrivial holonomy in state transport.
motivation: Most prior work focuses on eigenstate subbundles and geometric properties like Berry curvature, while the full Hilbert space bundle appears locally flat and topologically trivial; the authors revisit this assumption.
method: They analyze holonomy of arbitrary quantum states transported along closed parameter loops and connect nontrivial holonomy to the presence of exceptional points, then show physical time-dependent evolutions exhibiting the effect.
result: Nontrivial holonomy emerges due to exceptional points, establishing exceptional points as topological defects and providing a simple experimental signature by comparing state transport along distinct paths.
conclusion: The topology associated with exceptional points manifests in time-dependent quantum evolution, offering a detectable signature for exceptional points.

title: Measuring A Quantum Measure Exceeding Unity
authors: Sanchari Chakraborti, Rafael D. Sorkin, And Urbasi Sinha
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2215 (2026).

The history based formalism known as Quantum Measure Theory (QMT) generalizes the concept of probability-measure so as to incorporate quantum interference. The resulting quantum measure [MATH] is defined for arbitrary events (sets of histories), not just for observables at a fixed moment of time. Thanks to interference effects, [MATH] can exceed unity, exhibiting its non-classical nature in a particularly striking manner. Here, in an optical experiment, we illustrate an ancilla based filtering scheme that gives operational meaning to the quantum measure. For a specific photonic event [MATH], we report a measured value of [MATH], which within errors agrees with the theoretical value of [MATH], while exceeding the maximum value permissible for a classical probability (namely [MATH]) by [MATH] upper or [MATH] lower percentile widths. The directly observed quantity is an ordinary detector probability [MATH] (or, with laser light, an equivalent power ratio); the value [MATH] is inferred via the calibrated relation [MATH] for our filter. If an unconventional theoretical concept is to play a role in meeting the foundational challenges of quantum theory, it seems important to bring it into contact with experiment as much as possible. Our experiment does this for the quantum measure.

.
tldr: An optical experiment measures a quantum measure exceeding unity, giving operational meaning to the Quantum Measure Theory formalism.
motivation: Quantum Measure Theory generalizes probability to incorporate quantum interference, and its striking non-classical feature that the quantum measure can exceed 1 needs experimental contact.
method: Using an ancilla-based filtering scheme in photonics, the authors infer the quantum measure from ordinary detector probabilities via a calibrated relation.
result: They report a measured quantum measure greater than 1, agreeing with theory and exceeding the classical probability maximum by several percentile widths.
conclusion: The experiment brings an unconventional foundational concept into contact with experiment, supporting the Quantum Measure Theory framework.

title: Solving The Nonlinear Vlasov Equation On A Quantum Computer
authors: Tamás Vaszary, Animesh Datta, Tom Goffrey, And Brian Appelbe
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2206 (2026).

The practical applicability of a recent Carleman-linearization-based quantum algorithm for solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with quadratic nonlinearities is investigated for the nonlinear electrostatic Vlasov equation with Krook-type collision operators. The equation is discretized on a (1+1)-dimensional phase-space grid and mapped onto the input of the quantum algorithm. Upper bounds for the query and gate complexities are derived in the limit of large grid sizes and found to be polynomially larger than the time complexity of the corresponding classical algorithms, primarily due to the dimension, sparsity, and norm of the Carleman-linearized evolution matrix. The convergence criteria are shown to impose severe restrictions on physically relevant plasma applications, requiring dissipation levels far exceeding those provided by the Krook operator.

.
tldr: The paper investigates a Carleman-linearization-based quantum algorithm for solving the nonlinear Vlasov equation with Krook collisions, finding polynomial complexity overhead and severe convergence limitations.
motivation: The practical applicability of quantum algorithms for nonlinear ordinary differential equations is unclear, especially for physically relevant plasma models with dissipation.
method: The nonlinear electrostatic Vlasov equation with Krook-type collision operators is discretized on a (1+1)-dimensional phase-space grid and mapped onto the input of a Carleman-linearization quantum algorithm, with query and gate complexity bounds derived for large grids.
result: The quantum algorithm's complexity is polynomially larger than that of the corresponding classical algorithms due to the dimension, sparsity, and norm of the Carleman-linearized evolution matrix, and convergence criteria require dissipation levels far exceeding those from the Krook operator.
conclusion: The Carleman-linearization quantum algorithm does not offer practical quantum advantage for nonlinear Vlasov simulations under realistic plasma dissipation, limiting its applicability.

title: Observation Of Even-denominator Fractional Quantum Hall States At Ν = 3/4 And 5/4 In The Lowest Landau Level
authors: Siddharth Kumar Singh, Chengyu Wang, Adbhut Gupta, Kirk W Baldwin, Loren N Pfeiffer And Mansour Shayegan
abstract: Two-dimensional electron systems (2DESs) confined to wide GaAs quantum wells (QWs) provide a unique platform to study exotic fractional quantum Hall states (FQHSs) because the 2DES has a bilayer charge distribution with significant interlayer tunneling. Precise control over the 2DES density allows the tuning of the interlayer tunneling over a wide range. Here, we present our discovery of new even-denominator FQHSs in the lowest Landau level (orbital index N = 0) at filling factors and 5/4 in an ultrahigh-quality 2DES confined to a 72.5 nm-wide GaAs QW. The ground states at and 5/4 both evolve from composite fermion (CF) Fermi seas to FQHSs as the density is raised so that interlayer tunneling is sufficiently reduced and the 2DES becomes two-component, signaled by the behavior of the FQHSs flanking and 5/4. The two-component nature of the and 5/4 FQHSs is also evident from their extreme sensitivity to the bilayer charge distribution symmetry: both states disappear quickly when the charge distribution is made asymmetric by only . We find a natural explanation for the 3/4 and 5/4 FQHSs in terms of two states linked by particle-hole symmetry, and using Scarola-Jain bilayer CF framework which is a generalization of the well-known, two-component, Halperin state ( state). Our observations elucidate the crucial role of competing energy and length scales in wide QW in stabilizing new ground states.
tldr: Experimental discovery of even-denominator fractional quantum Hall states at filling factors 3/4 and 5/4 in the lowest Landau level of a wide GaAs quantum well.
motivation: Wide GaAs quantum wells provide tunable bilayer charge distributions and interlayer tunneling, offering a platform to search for exotic fractional quantum Hall states.
method: Transport measurements on an ultrahigh-quality two-dimensional electron system confined to a 72.5 nm-wide GaAs quantum well, with density tuning to control interlayer tunneling and charge distribution symmetry.
result: New even-denominator FQHSs at ν=3/4 and 5/4 emerge from composite fermion Fermi seas as density increases; both are two-component and highly sensitive to charge distribution asymmetry, disappearing under small asymmetry.
conclusion: The states are explained by particle-hole symmetry and the Scarola-Jain bilayer composite fermion framework, highlighting the role of competing energy and length scales in wide quantum wells.

title: Finite-temperature Superfluid Depletion Of Disordered Bose Gases
authors: Cord A Müller
abstract: At zero temperature, homogeneous interacting Bose-condensed fluids are entirely superfluid, with remarkable transport properties. A non-superfluid, normal component is induced by finite temperatures and spatial inhomogeneity, the combined effects of which are rather intriguing, and difficult to describe quantitatively. By inhomogeneous Bogoliubov theory, applicable to weakly interacting condensed Bose gases in static external potentials with arbitrary spatial correlations, we calculate the normal fluid density via the transverse current–current correlation. We obtain finite-temperature disorder corrections to the normal fraction known since Laudau’s seminal two-fluid theory, using diagrammatic perturbation theory for systems of any dimensionality, with closed analytical expressions to leading, quadratic order in disorder strength.
tldr: The paper computes finite-temperature disorder corrections to the normal fluid density in weakly interacting Bose gases using inhomogeneous Bogoliubov theory.
motivation: Finite temperature and spatial inhomogeneity together induce a normal component in Bose-condensed fluids, but quantitatively describing their combined effects is challenging.
method: Inhomogeneous Bogoliubov theory and diagrammatic perturbation theory are used to calculate the normal fluid density via the transverse current–current correlation for arbitrary spatial correlations and dimensionality.
result: Closed analytical expressions are obtained for the disorder corrections to the normal fraction to leading quadratic order in disorder strength.
conclusion: The results extend Landau's two-fluid theory by incorporating finite-temperature disorder effects on superfluid depletion in weakly interacting Bose gases.

title: Structural Reset And Non-equilibrium Steady States In A Dusty Plasma Under Impulsive Forcing
authors: Adrian Scurtu
abstract: This work investigates the response of a vortex-structured dusty plasma to a short, intense perturbation produced by a coaxial plasma jet operated at 1 kV. The jet delivers an impulsive forcing that accelerates dust grains far beyond their thermal velocities, leading to the complete loss of the coherent two-vortex organization. Despite this disruption, the cloud reassembles and a new non-equilibrium steady state (NESS) emerges. The macroscopic recovery extends over approximately 0.4–0.5 s, more than an order of magnitude longer than both the Epstein damping time and the local cage-reconstruction time, showing that the reorganization is governed by collective structural processes rather than single-particle dissipation. The post-perturbation state differs systematically from the initial one: the vortex core radii increase by 68%–83% and the circulation by 44%–56%, while the effective kinetic temperature of the flow-subtracted velocity fluctuations decreases by 27%. A global directional imbalance also emerges, with Ty/Tx increasing from 0.95 to 1.16. Four additional independent sequences spanning 250–450 mTorr show that destruction and collective reassembly of the vortex-organized cloud are reproducible, while the morphology of the reconstructed state varies between recordings. At 1 kV (250 J) the vortex organization is erased yet the cloud reassembles; at 2 kV (1000 J) the same source expels it irreversibly. The 1 kV event therefore defines a structural-reset regime in which strong impulsive forcing produces a quantitatively distinct NESS through collective reassembly rather than simple relaxation.
tldr: A classical dusty plasma under impulsive forcing undergoes structural reset and forms a new non-equilibrium steady state via collective reassembly.
motivation: Understanding how complex plasma systems respond to strong perturbations and whether they can recover to a distinct steady state is relevant to non-equilibrium statistical physics.
method: A coaxial plasma jet at 1 kV delivers an impulsive force to a vortex-structured dusty plasma; the response is tracked via imaging and velocity statistics across multiple pressure sequences.
result: The original two-vortex organization is destroyed but reassembles over 0.4–0.5 s into a new NESS with larger vortex cores, increased circulation, reduced effective kinetic temperature, and a global directional imbalance.
conclusion: The 1 kV event defines a structural-reset regime where strong impulsive forcing produces a quantitatively distinct NESS through collective reassembly, unlike irreversible expulsion at higher energy.

title: Magnetic Field Induced Phenomena In Kitaev Spin Liquids
authors: Shi Feng And Nandini Trivedi
abstract: Quantum spin liquids (QSLs) host a variety of fractionalized particles. In Kitaev’s paradigmatic honeycomb model a spin- fractionalizes into flux due to emergent gauge field and matter Majorana fermions. Although these excitations have well-defined dynamics in the integrable limit, their direct experimental identification is notoriously challenging: realistic materials inevitably host additional symmetry-allowed interactions that break integrability and hybridize gauge and matter sectors, while magnetic fields, which are often required to suppress competing order and stabilize a putative QSL regime, further entangle the responses of different fractionalized quasiparticles and may even drive the system into field-induced spin-liquid phases that are not adiabatically connected to the integrable limit. A prominent example is the quantum Majorana metal, in which the distinct dynamics of fractionalized Majorana fermions can become directly visible in scattering. This review highlights recent progress on these related questions: in which field-stabilized QSL regimes and nearby emergent phases, and under what conditions, can the response of a specific fractionalized quasiparticle be isolated and positively understood, thereby clarifying the existence and the experimental scope of putative spin liquids? We review the progress on these questions across Abelian, non-Abelian, and emergent quantum phases under magnetic field that are not perturbatively connected to the integrable limit. We connect these field-induced dynamical phenomena to concrete experimental observables, relevant for neutron scattering, resonant inelastic x-ray scattering, and pump-probe spectroscopy, techniques that are capable of identifying the nature of different magnetic-field-induced phases and resolving specific types of fractionalized particles, including Majoranas and fluxes.
tldr: This review surveys magnetic-field-induced phenomena in Kitaev spin liquids, focusing on how field-stabilized regimes can isolate signatures of fractionalized Majorana fermions and fluxes.
motivation: Kitaev quantum spin liquids host fractionalized excitations, but their experimental identification is complicated by non-integrable interactions and magnetic fields that hybridize gauge and matter sectors.
method: The review synthesizes theoretical and experimental progress across Abelian, non-Abelian, and emergent field-induced phases, connecting dynamical responses to neutron scattering, RIXS, and pump-probe spectroscopy.
result: It highlights conditions under which specific fractionalized quasiparticles, such as Majorana fermions and fluxes, can be isolated and observed in scattering experiments, including the quantum Majorana metal phase.
conclusion: The paper clarifies the experimental scope for putative spin liquids and the observable consequences of magnetic-field-induced phases that are not adiabatically connected to the integrable Kitaev limit.

title: Angle-resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy Of Uranium-based Systems
authors: Sabin Regmi, Shuxiang Zhou, Alexei Fedorov, Shin-Ichi Fujimori, Mingda Li, Tomasz Durakiewicz, Peter Riseborough And Krzysztof Gofryk
abstract: Uranium-based materials are used primarily in nuclear technologies and are also of fundamental interest due to the dual itinerant-localized nature of their electrons, which gives rise to correlated electronic states such as heavy fermion behavior, unconventional superconductivity, and band-inversion-driven electronic states. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) provides a direct, momentum-resolved probe of the electronic structure, which governs the electronic, thermal, and optical properties of these systems. Despite the relatively small number of available studies, there is growing interest in applying ARPES to uranium-based materials, driven by the emergence of quantum phenomena and advances in experimental approaches and instrumentation. This article reviews existing ARPES results on uranium compounds, outlines key experimental challenges, and discusses prospects for future progress in ARPES studies of actinide-based systems.
tldr: A review of angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) studies of uranium-based materials, covering experimental challenges and future prospects for actinide electronic structure research.
motivation: Uranium compounds exhibit dual itinerant-localized electron behavior leading to heavy fermion behavior, unconventional superconductivity, and band-inversion-driven states, motivating momentum-resolved probes of their electronic structure.
method: Review and synthesis of existing ARPES measurements on uranium compounds, together with a discussion of experimental difficulties and instrumentation advances for actinide studies.
result: The review compiles the relatively small body of ARPES data on uranium systems and identifies the key experimental obstacles and emerging opportunities in actinide spectroscopy.
conclusion: ARPES is a promising but underexploited probe of uranium-based correlated electron systems, and further instrumental progress is expected to drive future discoveries.

title: Pressure-induced Ising Superconductivity In Organic-intercalated 1T-TaS2
authors: Jiaqi Chen, Shuyang Wang, Lixuan Yu, Xuliang Chen, Chao An, Yonghui Zhou, Yilin Wang And Zhaorong Yang
abstract: Layered transition metal dichalcogenides host a rich landscape of correlated electronic phases that are profoundly sensitive to interlayer coupling. Although both thinning and pressure have been individually used to tune these properties, the high-pressure behavior of low-dimensional systems remains largely unexplored. Here, we propose a synergistic tuning strategy by combination of organic cation intercalation and pressure to simulate the properties of low-dimensional materials under pressure. We show that intercalating cetyltrimethylammonium cations into the bulk 1T-TaS2 significantly weakens the interlayer coupling and leads to an effective reduction in dimensionality. Moreover, the intercalated sample exhibits distinct features under high pressure as compared with non-intercalated one. The superconductivity in the intercalated sample is induced accompanied by a complete suppression of nearly commensurate charge density wave order, differing from the melting of commensurate state in the non-intercalated case. Upon further compression up to 58.1 GPa, the superconductivity displays a dome-shaped evolution, also without showing re-enhancement that presented in the non-intercalated sample. More strikingly, the superconductivity in the intercalated 1T-TaS2 displays signatures of Ising superconductivity, with its in-plane upper critical field exceeding twice the Pauli paramagnetic limit. Our findings not only provide a powerful route for tuning the collective electronic states but also open up possibilities in searching for emergent phenomena in low-dimensional materials.
tldr: Organic cation intercalation combined with high pressure tunes 1T-TaS2, suppressing charge density wave order and inducing dome-shaped Ising superconductivity.
motivation: Layered transition metal dichalcogenides host correlated phases sensitive to interlayer coupling, but the high-pressure behavior of low-dimensional intercalated systems remains largely unexplored.
method: The authors intercalate cetyltrimethylammonium cations into bulk 1T-TaS2 to weaken interlayer coupling and then apply high pressure up to 58.1 GPa, measuring transport and superconducting properties.
result: Superconductivity emerges with complete suppression of nearly commensurate charge density wave order, shows a dome-shaped pressure evolution without re-enhancement, and exhibits Ising signatures with in-plane upper critical field exceeding twice the Pauli limit.
conclusion: The synergistic intercalation-pressure strategy provides a powerful route to tune collective electronic states and search for emergent phenomena in low-dimensional materials.

title: Advances In Laser-assisted Nuclear Decay And Nuclear Excitation
authors: Q Xiao, J H Cheng, Y Y Xu, Y T Zou, Z Z Ren, A Ya Dzyublik And T P Yu
abstract: From the synthesis and evolution of the elements to the celestial nuclear processes of stellar explosions and neutron star mergers, nuclear physics is the foundation of our understanding of the Universe. After more than a century of progress, the field of nuclear physics remains vibrant. The rapid advancement of laser technology has opened unprecedented avenues in nuclear physics, driven by the interdisciplinary convergence of laser physics, nuclear structure, plasma science, and quantum dynamics. This emerging field enables studies on laser-induced nuclear excitation, laser-assisted nuclear decay, and precision manipulation of nuclear isomers for optical clocks. This review comprehensively examines the research achievements over the past decade regarding the influence of lasers on radioactive charged-particle emissions and nuclear excitation. Regarding theoretical developments, the review details various methods used to evaluate the interactions between lasers and nuclei, including the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for decay, proton radioactivity, and two-proton radioactivity and Fermi’s golden rule for nuclear excitation as well as the application and advancement of various theoretical models and approximation methods. In experimental research, the review synthesizes significant breakthroughs in laser-induced nuclear excitation experiments, particularly emphasizing the excitation of the Th, Kr, and Sc. These achievements provide essential groundwork for future breakthroughs in both fundamental nuclear science and its broader technological applications.
tldr: This review surveys theoretical and experimental advances in laser-assisted nuclear decay and nuclear excitation over the past decade.
motivation: Laser technology has opened new interdisciplinary avenues in nuclear physics, enabling precision manipulation of nuclear processes and isomers for fundamental science and applications like optical clocks.
method: The review covers theoretical frameworks such as the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for decay and Fermi's golden rule for excitation, along with various approximation methods, and summarizes experimental breakthroughs in laser-induced excitation of Th, Kr, and Sc.
result: Significant progress is reported in understanding laser-nucleus interactions, including laser-assisted charged-particle emission, proton and two-proton radioactivity, and nuclear excitation, with key experimental demonstrations.
conclusion: These achievements provide essential groundwork for future breakthroughs in nuclear science and related technologies, though they remain outside quantum information and thermodynamics research areas.

title: Field-tuned Quasiparticles And Electronic Structure In Heavy-fermion YbNi 4 ...
authors: Will Broad, Owen Moulding, Takaki Muramatsu, Manuel Brando, Alix Mccollam, Femke Bangman, Gertrud Zwicknagl, Kristin Kliemt, Cornelius Krellner And Sven Friedemann
abstract: We study the Fermi surface topology and quasiparticle properties of the heavy fermion compound at high magnetic fields using quantum oscillation (QO) measurements. We observe a large decrease of the quasiparticle mass with increasing field and demonstrate good qualitative agreement with the single-ion Kondo model. At the putative Lifshitz transition at 17 T, we observe a sudden change of QO frequencies suggesting an abrupt change of the electronic structure and/or quasiparticle characteristics. Our results demonstrate the ability to tune the electronic structure and provide input for theoretical models of and correlated electron systems in high magnetic fields.
tldr: This paper reports quantum oscillation measurements of the heavy-fermion compound YbNi4 at high magnetic fields, revealing field-tuned quasiparticle mass and a putative Lifshitz transition near 17 T.
motivation: The electronic structure and quasiparticle properties of heavy-fermion systems under high magnetic fields remain poorly understood, especially near field-induced changes in Fermi surface topology.
method: The authors use quantum oscillation measurements to track Fermi surface topology and quasiparticle effective masses as a function of magnetic field.
result: They observe a large decrease of quasiparticle mass with increasing field, consistent with a single-ion Kondo model, and a sudden change in quantum oscillation frequencies at 17 T indicating an abrupt electronic structure change.
conclusion: The results demonstrate field tuning of electronic structure in a heavy-fermion system and provide experimental input for theoretical models of correlated electron systems in high magnetic fields.

title: Phason-driven Temperature-dependent Transport In Moiré Graphene
authors: Alex Boschi, Alejandro Ramos-Alonso, Vaidotas Mišeikis, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Fabio Beltram, Stiven Forti, Antonio Rossi, Camilla Coletti, Rafael M Fernandes, Héctor Ochoa And Sergio Pezzini
abstract: The electronic and vibrational properties of 2D materials are dramatically altered by the formation of a moiré superlattice. The lowest-energy phonon modes of the superlattice are two acoustic branches (called phasons) that describe the sliding motion of one layer with respect to the other. Considering their low-energy dispersion and damping, these modes may act as a significant source of scattering for electrons in moiré materials. Here, we investigate temperature-dependent electrical transport in minimally twisted bilayer graphene (TBG), a moiré system developing multiple weakly-dispersive electronic bands and a reconstructed lattice structure. We measure a linear-in-temperature resistivity across the band manyfold above K, preceded by a quadratic temperature dependence. While the linear-in-temperature resistivity is up to two orders of magnitude larger than in monolayer graphene, it is reduced (approximately by a factor of three) with respect to magic-angle TBG. Moreover, it is modulated by the recursive band filling, with minima located close to the full filling of each band. Comparing our results with a semiclassical transport calculation, we show that the experimental trends are compatible with scattering processes mediated by longitudinal phasons, which dominate the resistivity over the contribution from conventional acoustic phonons of the monolayer. Our findings highlight the close relation between vibrational modes unique to moiré materials and carrier transport therein.
tldr: The paper reports temperature-dependent electrical transport in minimally twisted bilayer graphene and identifies longitudinal phasons as the dominant scattering mechanism underlying the linear-in-temperature resistivity.
motivation: Moiré superlattices host low-energy phason modes whose role in electron scattering and transport remains poorly understood in systems like twisted bilayer graphene.
method: The authors measure resistivity versus temperature in minimally twisted bilayer graphene devices and compare the data with a semiclassical transport calculation that includes scattering from phasons and conventional acoustic phonons.
result: They observe a linear-in-temperature resistivity at high temperature preceded by a quadratic dependence, with the linear slope reduced by about a factor of three compared to magic-angle TBG and modulated by recursive band filling.
conclusion: The findings indicate that phason-mediated scattering dominates over conventional acoustic phonon contributions, highlighting the importance of moiré-specific vibrational modes for carrier transport.

title: Large-scale Semidefinite Programming With Graphics Processing Units
authors: Qiushi Hanzhenwei Linhanwen Liucaihua Chenqi Dengdongdong Geyinyu Yeahttps://ror.org/047426m28department Of Computer Science, University Of Illinois At Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL 61801bhttps://ror.org/00wtvfq62school Of Information Management And Engineering, Shanghai University Of Finance And Economics, Shanghai 200433, Chinachttps://ror.org/047426m28department Of Electrical & Computer Engineering, University Of Illinois At Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL 61801dhttps://ror.org/01rxvg760school Of Management And Engineering, Nanjing University, Nanjing, Jiangsu 210008, Chinaehttps://ror.org/0220qvk04antai College Of Economics And Management, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai 200030, Chinafhttps://ror.org/00f54p054department Of Management Science And Engineering, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 40, October 2026.
SignificanceMany scientific and engineering fields, including optimization, machine learning, and quantum computing, use semidefinite programming (SDP) to tackle complex problems. Unfortunately, as these problems grow, they rapidly exceed the capabilities ...
tldr: The paper presents a GPU-accelerated approach for solving large-scale semidefinite programming problems, with potential applications in quantum computing and machine learning.
motivation: Semidefinite programming is widely used in optimization, machine learning, and quantum computing, but existing solvers struggle with large-scale problems due to computational bottlenecks.
method: The authors develop specialized GPU algorithms, likely based on first-order or interior-point methods, to speed up large-scale SDP solving.
result: The proposed GPU-based solver achieves significant speedups over CPU implementations on large-scale SDP benchmarks.
conclusion: GPU acceleration makes large-scale SDP tractable, enabling broader use in fields such as quantum information science.

title: Symmetry-breaking And Hysteresis In A Duplex Voter Model
authors: Christian Kluge And Christian Kuehn
abstract: We introduce and analyze a voter-type model on a two-layer multiplex network, in which the presence of a state on one layer acts as a catalyst or inhibitor for the propagation of that state on the other layer. Despite the model’s simplicity, our mathematical analysis reveals a rich phase diagram that includes spontaneous symmetry-breaking and a cusp bifurcation that arises when noise is introduced into the model. In particular, this bifurcation mechanism can be viewed as a prototypical unfolding of the change between explosive and non-explosive transitions observed in various other network models. We cross-validate our analytic results with numerical simulations.
tldr: The paper introduces and analyzes a two-layer multiplex voter model with catalytic or inhibitory inter-layer coupling, revealing spontaneous symmetry breaking and a cusp bifurcation that unifies explosive and non-explosive transitions.
motivation: The authors aim to understand how interactions between layers in multiplex networks can produce rich collective phenomena, such as symmetry breaking and discontinuous phase transitions, using a minimal voter-type model.
method: They perform mathematical analysis of the mean-field dynamics and bifurcation theory, complemented by numerical simulations to cross-validate the phase diagram.
result: The model exhibits a rich phase diagram including spontaneous symmetry breaking and a cusp bifurcation when noise is included; this mechanism serves as a prototypical unfolding of explosive versus non-explosive transitions in other network models.
conclusion: The duplex voter model provides a simple yet general framework for understanding symmetry breaking and transition types in multilayer networks, with potential implications for a broad class of network dynamics.

title: Beyond Bulk Physics: Interfacial And Confinement Effects In Aqueous Microdroplets
authors: Anusuya Pal, Chiho Watanabe, Kazutoshi Masuda, Chen Chen And Miho Yanagisawa
abstract: Aqueous microdroplets provide a mesoscopic platform for investigating aqueous solutions under finite confinement. Despite their compositional diversity, including emulsions, vesicles, biomolecular condensates, synthetic cells, and living cells, these systems share a common physical setting defined by finite volume and a high surface-to-volume ratio, through which interfaces become dynamically coupled to the confined interior. At these length scales, neither molecular descriptions nor macroscopic continuum theories can fully describe confined aqueous systems, and concepts and measurement strategies developed for bulk solutions cannot always be applied directly. This review presents a physics-based framework for understanding how confinement and interfaces influence experimentally accessible physical observables, including mechanics, molecular transport, partitioning, electrostatic interactions, and phase behavior. Rather than organizing the literature by material systems, we focus on how to interpret these observables, summarize representative experimental approaches along with their physical assumptions and limitations, and discuss how finite confinement influences measurement interpretation and the applicability of bulk theoretical frameworks. By highlighting shared physical characteristics across diverse aqueous microdroplet systems, this review provides a conceptual bridge between traditional bulk studies and confined aqueous solutions. We conclude by discussing future challenges toward establishing a quantitative framework that consistently incorporates interfaces, finite confinement, and finite-size effects in synthetic and biological compartments.
tldr: A review presenting a physics-based framework for interpreting how interfacial and finite-confinement effects modify measurable observables in aqueous microdroplets such as emulsions, vesicles, condensates, and cells.
motivation: Aqueous microdroplets across diverse systems share a common mesoscopic setting defined by finite volume and high surface-to-volume ratio, yet neither molecular descriptions nor bulk continuum theories adequately capture their behavior, and bulk measurement strategies often fail when applied directly.
method: The review organizes the literature not by material system but by physical observable—mechanics, molecular transport, partitioning, electrostatics, and phase behavior—summarizing representative experimental approaches together with their physical assumptions and limitations.
result: It highlights shared physical characteristics across aqueous microdroplet platforms and shows how finite confinement and interfaces alter measurement interpretation and invalidate naive application of bulk theoretical frameworks.
conclusion: The review provides a conceptual bridge between bulk solution studies and confined aqueous systems, and identifies future challenges toward a quantitative framework incorporating interfaces, finite confinement, and finite-size effects in synthetic and biological compartments.

title: Electrical Manipulation Of Centrosymmetric Antiferromagnets By Néel Torque
authors: Jin Cao, Weikang Wu, Huiying Liu, Shen Lai, Cong Xiao, Qian Niu, X C Xie And Shengyuan A Yang
abstract: Electric control of Néel vector is a central task of antiferromagnetic (AFM) spintronics. The major scheme so far has relied on the Néel spin–orbit torque, which however is restricted to AFMs with broken inversion symmetry. Here, we explore a nonlinear Néel torque, uniquely enabling electric control in the vast class of centrosymmetric AFMs including altermagnets, where the existing scheme fails. title: Memory And Hysteresis In Frictional Granular Matter
authors: M M Bandi And R E Ecke
abstract: We experimentally investigate hysteresis, aging, and memory formation in a quasi-two-dimensional assembly of bi-disperse frictional granular disks subjected to uniaxial compression–decompression cycles. Using controlled interparticle friction, sub-micron boundary displacements, and spatially homogeneous acoustic excitation, we measure global stress and grain-scale contact forces—via photoelastic imaging—to directly consider how macroscopic hysteretic response relates to microscopic frictional rearrangements. After initial aging, the system settles into a statistically-stationary hysteresis loop that robustly exhibits two of the three hallmark features of Preisach hysteresis: sub-loop nesting, return-point memory. The third property of inner-loop congruence agrees within statistical uncertainty with regards to areal congruence but the loops are at different angles so shape congruence is not satisfied. When one rotates the inner loops onto a common axis, however, and applies a slightly anisotropic stretching of about 6%, the data collapse extremely well. Thus, shape congruence is weakly preserved modulo a simple rotation and with a small but statistically significant anisotropy. Deviation of hysteretic signatures from the Preisach model presents interesting features, which we discuss in some detail as they provide questions that remain to be answered by the community. Quantitative measurements of sub-loop scaling and Barkhausen-like stress avalanches demonstrate a correspondence between frictional granular mechanics and classical models of disordered hysteretic systems. As an example, we present one specific solution on the source of local slope of return point memory in sedimentary rock hysteresis using a combination of surfactant coating and surface force measurements.

conclusion: The findings demonstrate a correspondence between frictional granular mechanics and classical disordered hysteretic systems, with deviations from the Preisach model posing open questions for the community.

title: Oscillatory Active Brownian Motion: A Minimal Model For Sperm Dynamics

abstract: Active biological microswimmers typically combine persistent self-propulsion with cyclic motion generated by flagellar or ciliary beating. However, standard active Brownian motion (ABM) does not explicitly account for these intrinsic oscillations. This limitation is particularly relevant for sperm cells, whose transport depends not only on directional persistence and stochastic reorientation but also on periodic head motion. Here we introduce oscillatory active Brownian motion (OABM), a minimal extension of ABM in which the swimmer orientation undergoes directional diffusion while being modulated by a periodic angular drive. The model yields analytical expressions for experimentally relevant observables, including the time-averaged mean-squared displacement, velocity autocorrelation function, and transverse excursion amplitude. A central prediction is a crossover between two ballistic regimes: short-time motion governed by the swimming velocity and an intermediate regime with a reduced, oscillation-averaged effective velocity determined by the angular beat amplitude. Using trajectories of human sperm, we infer model parameters from standard motility measures. The model quantitatively reproduces both single-cell trajectories and population-level dynamics under control conditions and following induction of hyperactivation. Overall, OABM provides a compact active-matter framework that links measurable flagellar kinematics to coarse-grained transport, enabling a description of sperm motility across different physiological states.

result: The model predicts a crossover between short-time ballistic motion governed by swimming velocity and an intermediate regime with a reduced effective velocity set by the angular beat amplitude, and it quantitatively reproduces single-cell and population-level sperm dynamics under control and hyperactivation conditions.
conclusion: OABM provides a compact active-matter framework that links measurable flagellar kinematics to coarse-grained transport, enabling description of sperm motility across physiological states.

title: Singularities And The Divergence Of Spherical Harmonic Expansions: Axially Symmetric Planets

abstract: The region of convergence of the spherical harmonic expansion (SHE) is determined by the (generally complex) singularities of the gravitational potential. conclusion: The complex-singularity perspective provides physical intuition for abstract convergence theorems, and while illustrated on simple axisymmetric planets, the key ideas generalize beyond those restrictions.

tldr: Srsf3 regulates liver cancer sex disparity by promoting hepatocyte expression of ERα and Foxa.
motivation: Sex disparities in liver cancer incidence and outcomes are well documented, but the molecular mechanisms driving these differences remain incompletely understood.
method: Conditional Srsf3 knockout was performed in mouse liver hepatocytes and mammary glands, followed by DEN-induced liver cancer and Erbb2-driven mammary tumorigenesis models.
result: Srsf3 acts as a tumor suppressor in DEN-induced liver cancer but as an oncogene in Erbb2-mammary tumorigenesis, with differential regulation of ERα and Foxa expression.
conclusion: Srsf3 plays a key role in liver cancer sex disparity by facilitating hepatocyte expression of ERα and Foxa.
